title: Testing for a unit root
objectives: Run an augmented Dickey-Fuller test and read its result.
Explain why the test uses its own critical values and why a non-rejection is weak evidence.

screens.title: Which one is the walk?
screens.prose: Two seeded series of 500 days. One is a random walk, $x_t = x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$. The other is an AR(1), $x_t = 0.9\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, which pulls back towards 0. The shocks have sd 1 in both.
screens.question: Tap the random walk.

hints.text: A walk has nothing pulling it back. Which series keeps crossing 0?
The bottom series crosses its zero line again and again.
The top one drifts to about −20 and stays away for hundreds of days: the walk.

feedback.correct: That's it. The top series is the walk.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the series that never seems to come home.

byKey.right: You tapped the series that keeps crossing 0. With $\phi = 0.9$ a shock halves in under a week, so it returns quickly.

explain.text: With $\phi = 0.9$ a shock halves in $\ln 0.5/\ln 0.9 \approx 6.6$ days, so the bottom series crosses 0 dozens of times. The walk has no pull at all. Last lesson's $\phi = 0.95$ over 250 days was harder; we need a test that works when the eye fails.

screens.title: The test regression
screens.prose: Subtract $x_{t-1}$ from both sides of $x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$: $$\Delta x_t = (\phi - 1)\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t = \gamma\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t.$$ A walk has $\phi = 1$, a **unit root**, so $\gamma = 0$. The **Dickey-Fuller test** regresses $\Delta x_t$ on a constant and $x_{t-1}$ and tests $H_0: \gamma = 0$ against $\gamma < 0$.

state.caption: Least squares of $\Delta x_t$ on a constant and $x_{t-1}$, 499 days.

screens.question: What is the t statistic for $\hat\gamma$? Give 2 decimal places.

hints.text: A t statistic is an estimate over its standard error.
Use the $x_{t-1}$ row.

feedback.correct: Correct. $t = -5.05$: $\hat\gamma$ sits about five standard errors below 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the coefficient on $x_{t-1}$ by its standard error.

byKey.flip: You divided the standard error by the coefficient. The estimate goes on top.
byKey.pos: You dropped the sign. $\hat\gamma$ is negative, so $t$ is too, and only negative values count against $H_0$.
byKey.phi: You gave $\hat\phi = 1 + \hat\gamma$. The test uses the t statistic of $\hat\gamma$.

explain.text: $\hat\gamma = -0.0976$, so $\hat\phi = 1 + \hat\gamma = 0.902$, close to the true 0.9. Its t statistic is -5.05. Whether that is far enough from 0 depends on the distribution of $t$ when $\gamma = 0$, which is the surprise of this lesson.

screens.title: Dickey-Fuller by hand
screens.prose: Build the test regression with NumPy. The design matrix has a column of ones for the constant and a column of yesterday's values; the t statistic is $\hat\gamma$ over its standard error.
screens.question: Complete `df_t_stat(x)`.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def df_t_stat(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dx = np.diff(x)                                     # Δx_t
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dx)), ...])        # constant and x_{t-1}
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, dx, rcond=None)[0]
    resid = dx - X @ beta
    s2 = resid @ resid / (len(dx) - 2)
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])
    return ...                                          # t statistic of gamma
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def df_t_stat(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    dx = np.diff(x)                                     # Δx_t
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(dx)), x[:-1]])     # constant and x_{t-1}
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X, dx, rcond=None)[0]
    resid = dx - X @ beta
    s2 = resid @ resid / (len(dx) - 2)
    se = np.sqrt(s2 * np.linalg.inv(X.T @ X)[1, 1])
    return beta[1] / se

hints.text: The second column is yesterday: `x[:-1]`.
Row $t$ pairs $\Delta x_t$ with $x_{t-1}$.
Fill `x[:-1]` and `return beta[1] / se`.

feedback.correct: Correct. On the bottom series you get -5.0522, as statsmodels' `adfuller(x, maxlag=0, regression="c")` does.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Regress $\Delta x_t$ on ones and `x[:-1]`, then divide the slope by its standard error.

explain.text: `adfuller(x, maxlag=0, regression="c", autolag=None)` returns -5.0522 for the bottom series, the same regression with no lagged differences. The constant makes the statistic blind to the series' level, which the test adding 50 checks. Without a constant, a series with a mean far from 0 would look like a walk.

screens.title: Not a t distribution
screens.prose: Simulate 2,000 seeded random walks of 250 days, so $H_0$ is true, and compute each one's Dickey-Fuller $t$. The bars are those 2,000 statistics. The curve is the $N(0, 1)$ density that an ordinary t test would use. Bars left of −1.645 are recoloured.
screens.question: About what share of the 2,000 walks have $t$ below −1.645, the one-sided 5% point of the normal?

options.text: About 5%
options.why: You trusted the normal curve. Count the recoloured bars: they hold far more than 100 of the 2,000 walks.

options.text: About 20%
options.why: Look where the bars peak: near −1.5, already close to the cut. Almost half the walks lie left of it.

options.text: About 45%
About 90%
options.why: Some walks give $t$ above 0, and the peak is near −1.5, just right of the cut. Fewer than half lie left of it.

hints.text: Where do the bars peak, compared with the curve?
The bars sit well left of the curve.
The bars peak near −1.5, right beside the cut, so close to half lie beyond it: 45.2%.

feedback.correct: Correct. 45.25% of the walks fall below −1.645, nine times the 5% the normal promises.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the bars with the curve, then judge how much lies left of the cut.

byKey.five: You used the normal 5% point. Under a unit root the statistic is shifted left, so −1.645 would reject a true walk almost half the time.

explain.text: Under $H_0$ the statistic follows the **Dickey-Fuller distribution**: shifted left, with mean -1.52 here. 45.25% of true walks fall below −1.645, so the normal cut-off would reject a walk nearly half the time. The 5% point of these 2,000 is -2.89.

screens.title: Critical values by simulation
screens.prose: Dickey and Fuller tabulated these quantiles by simulation; MacKinnon (1996) refined them, and statsmodels uses his values. With a constant and large $n$ they are about −3.43 at 1%, −2.86 at 5% and −2.57 at 10% (Hyndman, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, section 9.1).
screens.question: Complete `df_null_quantile(n, sims, q, seed)`: simulate `sims` walks of `n` days and return the `q` quantile of their $t$ statistics.

widget.starter:
import numpy as np

def df_t_many(W):
    """Dickey-Fuller t statistic (with a constant) for each row of W."""
    dx = np.diff(W, axis=1)
    xl = W[:, :-1]
    m = dx.shape[1]
    xm = xl.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    ym = dx.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sxx = ((xl - xm) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    b = ((xl - xm) * (dx - ym)).sum(axis=1) / sxx
    a = ym[:, 0] - b * xm[:, 0]
    resid = dx - a[:, None] - b[:, None] * xl
    s2 = (resid ** 2).sum(axis=1) / (m - 2)
    return b / np.sqrt(s2 / sxx)

    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    walks = ...      # sims random walks of n days, one per row
    t = df_t_many(walks)
    return ...       # the q quantile of t, rounded to 2 places
widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def df_t_many(W):
    """Dickey-Fuller t statistic (with a constant) for each row of W."""
    dx = np.diff(W, axis=1)
    xl = W[:, :-1]
    m = dx.shape[1]
    xm = xl.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    ym = dx.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sxx = ((xl - xm) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    b = ((xl - xm) * (dx - ym)).sum(axis=1) / sxx
    a = ym[:, 0] - b * xm[:, 0]
    resid = dx - a[:, None] - b[:, None] * xl
    s2 = (resid ** 2).sum(axis=1) / (m - 2)
    return b / np.sqrt(s2 / sxx)

def df_null_quantile(n, sims, q, seed):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    walks = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal((sims, n)), axis=1)   # one walk per row
    t = df_t_many(walks)
    return round(float(np.quantile(t, q)), 2)

Each row is one walk, so sum along `axis=1`.
`walks = np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal((sims, n)), axis=1)` and `return round(float(np.quantile(t, q)), 2)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. 2,000 walks of 250 days give -3.43, -2.89 and -2.59.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Draw a `(sims, n)` array of shocks, take the running sum along each row, then the quantile.

explain.text: Your 2,000 walks give -3.43, -2.89 and -2.59, close to MacKinnon's large-sample −3.43, −2.86 and −2.57; 250 days is not quite large, and 2,000 walks leave some noise. A trend term shifts them further left: about −3.41 at 5%.

screens.title: Reading the result
screens.prose: `adfuller` on a seeded spread of 500 days returns the statistic -2.70, a p-value of 0.073, 0 lagged differences, and critical values -3.44, -2.87 and -2.57. We reject $H_0$ when the statistic is below the critical value.
screens.question: Tap every critical value at which this test rejects a unit root.

hints.text: Reject when the statistic lies to the left of the critical value.
Compare the statistic with the 5% and 10% points.
-2.70 is left of -2.57 but right of -2.87.

feedback.correct: Correct. Reject at 10%, not at 5%, matching the p-value of 0.073.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A critical value counts only if the statistic is further left than it.

byKey.normal: You counted the normal 5% point. The statistic beats it easily, but that cut-off rejects true walks nearly half the time.
byKey.five: The statistic, -2.70, is right of the 5% value -2.87. It does not reach it.
byKey.nrm: You used the normal cut-off. The Dickey-Fuller distribution needs the shifted values.

explain.text: The p-value 0.073 lies between 0.05 and 0.10, so the test rejects at 10% and not at 5%. The spread is in fact an AR(1) with $\phi = 0.97$: stationary, but only weakly detected in 500 days. Fix the level before you look.

screens.title: The augmented test
screens.prose: Real series have memory in their changes too. The **augmented** Dickey-Fuller test adds lagged changes to the regression to mop it up, and `autolag="AIC"` chooses how many. `adfuller` returns a tuple: statistic, p-value, lags used, observations, critical values.
screens.question: Complete `adf_decision(x, alpha)`: return the statistic, the p-value, and whether to reject at level `alpha`.

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

    stat, p = ..., ...
    return round(float(stat), 4), round(float(p), 4), ...   # reject when p < alpha

screens.title: How often does it catch reversion?
screens.prose: The **power** of the test is the chance it rejects when the series really is stationary (Hypothesis Testing, lesson 6). Simulate it: many seeded AR(1) paths with a chosen $\phi$, and the share whose $t$ falls below −2.86.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def df_t_many(W):
    """Dickey-Fuller t statistic (with a constant) for each row of W."""
    dx = np.diff(W, axis=1)
    xl = W[:, :-1]
    m = dx.shape[1]
    xm = xl.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    ym = dx.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sxx = ((xl - xm) ** 2).sum(axis=1)
    b = ((xl - xm) * (dx - ym)).sum(axis=1) / sxx
    a = ym[:, 0] - b * xm[:, 0]
    resid = dx - a[:, None] - b[:, None] * xl
    s2 = (resid ** 2).sum(axis=1) / (m - 2)
    return b / np.sqrt(s2 / sxx)

def adf_power(phi, n, sims, seed):
    e = np.random.default_rng(seed).standard_normal((sims, n))
    X = np.empty_like(e)
    X[:, 0] = e[:, 0]
    for t in range(1, n):
        X[:, t] = phi * X[:, t - 1] + e[:, t]       # all sims at once
    t_stats = df_t_many(X)
    return round(float(np.mean(t_stats < -2.86)), 2)

hints.text: Each column of `X` is one day for every path at once.
The recursion is the AR(1) model, applied to whole columns.
`X[:, t] = phi * X[:, t - 1] + e[:, t]` and `return round(float(np.mean(t_stats < -2.86)), 2)`.

feedback.correct: Correct. At $\phi = 0.8$ the power is 1.0; at 0.98 it is 0.12.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Update every path with the AR(1) rule, then count the share of $t$ below −2.86.

explain.text: At $\phi = 1.0$ the rate is 0.05: the size, close to 5% (slightly above, because −2.86 is the large-sample value). At $\phi = 0.98$, 250 days catch the reversion in only 12% of paths; 1,000 days raise that to 85%.

screens.title: Not rejected is not proven
screens.prose: The power curve from your simulation: 2,000 paths of 250 days at each $\phi$. A colleague tests a spread over 250 days, gets p = 0.45 and writes: "No rejection, so the spread has a unit root. Do not trade it."
screens.question: If the spread is really an AR(1) with $\phi = 0.98$, how often would this test reject? Give a decimal.

hints.text: Find $\phi = 0.98$ on the axis and read up to the curve.
The dashed vertical line marks 0.98.
The curve at 0.98 is at 0.12.

feedback.correct: Correct. About 12%: the test misses a real but slow reversion nearly nine times in ten.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the height of the curve where $\phi = 0.98$.

byKey.size: That is the rate at $\phi = 1$, the size of the test. At 0.98 the curve is a little higher.
byKey.certain: That is the power at $\phi = 0.9$ or below. Close to 1 the test barely tells $\phi$ apart from 1.
byKey.p: You reused the p-value. The question is how often the test rejects when $\phi = 0.98$, which the curve shows.

explain.text: With 250 days the test rejects a $\phi = 0.98$ series only 12% of the time, so failing to reject is the expected outcome even when the spread reverts. A non-rejection is absence of evidence, not evidence of a unit root. Last lesson's $\phi = 0.95$ series gives p = 0.45 too.

screens.title: The mirror test
screens.prose: The **KPSS test** swaps the roles: its null is that the series *is* stationary. statsmodels' `kpss` reports p-values only between 0.01 and 0.10, so it prints the bound when the true p is beyond it.
screens.question: What do the two tests say about the walk together?

options.text: They agree: ADF cannot reject a unit root, and KPSS rejects stationarity
They disagree: one p-value is large and the other small
options.why: You compared p-values without their nulls. A large ADF p and a small KPSS p point the same way, because the nulls are opposite.

options.text: KPSS shows the walk is stationary
options.why: You read KPSS like ADF. A small KPSS p rejects stationarity.

options.text: Nothing: neither test can say anything about a walk
options.why: KPSS rejects its null at 1%, which is a clear statement.

hints.text: Write down each test's null first.
ADF: unit root. KPSS: stationary.
ADF does not reject a unit root; KPSS rejects stationarity. Both say walk.

feedback.correct: Correct. Opposite nulls, the same conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read each p-value against its own null.

byKey.clash: You compared p-values without their nulls. ADF large and KPSS small is agreement.

explain.text: When ADF rejects and KPSS does not (the AR(1)), or ADF does not and KPSS does (the walk), the evidence is consistent. When both fail to reject, the data are too short or too ambiguous to decide. Running both is a cheap guard against low power.

screens.title: The ADF test
screens.prose: You ran the regression $$\Delta x_t = \alpha + \gamma\,x_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \delta_i\,\Delta x_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t,$$ tested $H_0: \gamma = 0$ (a unit root) against $\gamma < 0$, and compared $t$ with Dickey-Fuller critical values: about −2.86 at 5% with a constant, −3.41 with a constant and a trend.
screens.question: A series shows a steady upward trend. Which regression should the test use?

options.text: A constant and a trend, with the −3.41 critical value
A constant only, with −2.86
options.why: You left out the trend. A stationary series around a trend then looks like a walk, and the test fails to reject wrongly.

options.text: No constant and no trend
options.why: Without a constant the test assumes the series hovers around 0. Any series with a mean far from 0 then looks like a walk.

options.text: A constant only, with −1.645
options.why: −1.645 is the normal value. Under a unit root it rejects true walks almost half the time.

feedback.correct: Correct. Match the deterministic terms to what the data show.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The regression must include whatever the series does besides wander.

explain.text: The constant lets the series have a non-zero mean; the trend lets it have a straight-line drift. Each extra term shifts the critical values left. Including a trend that is not there costs power; leaving out one that is there biases the test towards a unit root.

screens.title: What a p-value of 0.29 says
screens.prose: A desk tests every candidate spread before trading it as mean-reverting (the Cointegration course). One spread, 500 days, gives an ADF statistic of -2.00 and p = 0.29. In an interview you are asked what that p-value tells you.
screens.question: Which answer is honest?

options.text: We cannot reject a unit root at 5%; with slow reversion the test has little power, so this is weak evidence either way, and we should not trade it as mean-reverting yet
There is a 29% chance the spread has a unit root
options.why: You read the p-value as the chance $H_0$ is true (Hypothesis Testing, lesson 7). It is the chance of a statistic this extreme if there were a unit root.

options.text: The spread has a unit root, so it is a random walk
options.why: You read non-rejection as proof. The power curve showed the test misses slow reversion most of the time.

options.text: The spread is stationary at the 29% level
options.why: Rejecting needs a small p-value. A p of 0.29 rejects nothing at any usual level.

hints.text: What is the null, and did we reject it?
Recall the power at $\phi = 0.98$.
Fail to reject, low power, so no strong conclusion, and no trade on this evidence.

feedback.correct: Correct. Fail to reject, say why that is weak evidence, and say what you would do.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The p-value is about the data under $H_0$, and a non-rejection proves nothing.

byKey.prob: You treated the p-value as a probability of the hypothesis. It is computed assuming the hypothesis is true.
byKey.proof: You read a non-rejection as proof of a unit root. With low power that is the usual result even for reverting spreads.

explain.text: This spread is the seeded walk from the start of the lesson, so here the cautious answer is also the right trade: none. Add that KPSS, a longer sample or an economic reason for the spread to revert would strengthen the case.

ideas: Write the AR(1) as $\Delta x_t = \gamma x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$ with $\gamma = \phi - 1$. A unit root is $\gamma = 0$; the Dickey-Fuller test is the t test of that.
Under a unit root the $t$ statistic is shifted left: use about −2.86 at 5% with a constant (−3.41 with a trend), never −1.645. `adfuller` adds lagged changes and gives the p-value.

Power is low near $\phi = 1$: with 250 days the test catches $\phi = 0.98$ only about 12% of the time. Not rejecting is not proof of a unit root; KPSS, with the opposite null, is a useful second opinion.

formula.name: Augmented Dickey-Fuller regression
formula.note: Reject a unit root when $t$ is below the Dickey-Fuller critical value.

summary.trap: A large ADF p-value does not prove a unit root, and the normal critical value −1.645 rejects true walks almost half the time.

quiz.prose: An ADF test with a constant on 1,000 days gives $t = -2.40$.
quiz.question: What do you conclude at the 5% level?

options.text: Fail to reject a unit root: −2.40 is not below −2.86
Reject: −2.40 is below −1.645
options.why: You used the normal critical value. The Dickey-Fuller 5% value with a constant is about −2.86.

options.text: Reject at 5%, because it rejects at 10%
options.why: −2.40 does not even reach the 10% value, −2.57.

options.text: The series is a random walk
options.why: Failing to reject is not proof of a unit root.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare with the Dickey-Fuller value, not the normal one.

explain.text: With a constant the 5% critical value is about −2.86 and the 10% value about −2.57. −2.40 reaches neither, so we fail to reject, and say so without claiming a unit root.

quiz.prose: A stationary series hovers around 5 with sd 1. An analyst runs the Dickey-Fuller test with no constant: `regression="n"`.
quiz.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: With no constant the test treats every distance from 0 as memory, so the series looks like a walk
Nothing: the constant only matters for trends
options.why: The constant is what lets the series have a non-zero mean. Without it the regression explains the mean of 5 with $x_{t-1}$.

options.text: It rejects too often
options.why: It is biased the other way: $\hat\gamma$ is pulled towards 0, so it rejects too rarely.

options.text: It should have used a trend instead
options.why: There is no trend. A constant is what this series needs.

feedback.correct: Correct. Always include the constant unless the series truly centres on 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how a regression with no constant can explain a mean of 5.

explain.text: $\Delta x_t = \gamma x_{t-1}$ with no intercept must fit a series that sits at 5 while changing by about 0 a day, which forces $\hat\gamma$ towards 0. The constant soaks up the mean, so the default `regression="c"` is the safe one.

quiz.prose: A new spread has 30 days of history. The ADF test gives p = 0.62.
quiz.question: What is the best reading?

options.text: The test says almost nothing: 30 days give it next to no power
The spread is a random walk
options.why: Non-rejection with 30 days is what almost any slow spread would give.

options.text: There is a 62% chance of a unit root
options.why: A p-value is not the probability of the null.

options.text: Run the test daily until it rejects

explain.text: With 30 observations only a very fast reversion would be detected. Wait for more data, and decide the test and sample length in advance.
